content: A Rice Krispie treat is a confectionery dessert or snack that is primarily composed of Rice Krispies cereal, melted margarine or butter, and melted marshmallows. Occasionally, seasonal marshmallows or cereals are incorporated to create holiday-themed variations of the treat. While these snacks are frequently prepared at home, they are also commercially available in stores, often sold under the Rice Krispies brand name. Numerous adaptations of the traditional Rice Krispie treat exist. For instance, caramel can be used as a substitute for marshmallows, or condensed milk can be added to the mixture prior to incorporating the Rice Krispies. Other variations include the use of corn syrup and peanut butter, the addition of mandarin oranges or vanilla, and more. A notable alternative involves replacing marshmallows with chocolate, resulting in a variation known as Chocolate Crackles. Kellogg's has since introduced commercially produced versions of both the marshmallow-based and chocolate-based treats, marketed under the name Rice Krispies Squares. The origin of Rice Krispie treats dates back to 1928, when Mildred Day, an employee of the Kellogg Company, created the snack. She developed the recipe as part of a fundraising effort for a Camp Fire Girls group. Mildred Day passed away in June 1996 at the age of 92. Kellogg's later introduced a cereal inspired by the Rice Krispie treat, marking what may be the first instance of a cereal being derived from a dessert that was itself based on a cereal. This product, known as Kellogg's Rice Krispies Treats cereal, experienced a brief surge in popularity and received a high rating of 6 out of 7 on the breakfast review website Mr. Breakfast. However, the cereal has become increasingly difficult to locate in recent years. Kellogg's website provides resources to assist consumers in finding their less commonly available cereals. For related variations, Chocolate Crackles is a version of the treat that incorporates cocoa and coconut, while Sachima is another similar confection.
